title: I Posted the Accordion-Bellows Hours After They Camped My Numbered Straps

parts.text: I stepped into the reed room at 5:09 p.m. and mentor Cleo was already using numbered gear. The board said: ONE BOX. SIXTY MINUTES. STRAPS STAY WITH THE SLOT. I was thirty-one, studio secretary, holding a checkout that listed our numbered straps. Cleo shrugged. "Mentors are the bellows." I photographed the board, the booking, and her leftover palettes on my numbered straps. Then I asked for the bellows log. At 5:17 the desk pinged why Cleo's name was on my palettes. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The desk can see Cleo's leftover palettes on my numbered straps.

social.video_title: They camped my numbered accordion straps — Part 1/2
social.description: Reed room, leftover palettes, a sixty-minute clock she posted. I logged the bellows. Would you have asked for the bellows log?

parts.text: Cleo called it bellows warm-up until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the palette still. The straps went back to my numbered slot. Cleo ran a slot of her own and told the next mentor atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: MENTORS ARE NOT THE BELLOWS. I keep my straps on a labeled peg. Cleo brown-bags her warm-ups. The reed room finally looks like a slot, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Mentors are not the bellows — Part 2/2
social.description: Bellows log, numbered straps, and a second line on the board. Was a warm-up ever my palettes?
